claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a designed hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale precipitates, coarse secondary phases, and tailored grain boundaries.
The hierarchical heterostructure produces reproducible mesoscopic features suitable for use as model descriptors.
A machine-learning framework can integrate imaging-derived and microanalysis-derived mesoscopic descriptors with limited full-scale simulations and tensile data.
The arrangement of secondary phases and grain boundaries mediates local plasticity and stress transfer.
The hierarchical arrangement homogenizes the macroscopic mechanical response.
Stable hierarchical features decouple local deformation from crack-initiation mechanisms.
Effective mesoscale descriptors permit prediction of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior without resolving the complete microstructure.
Using effective mesoscale descriptors reduces computational cost relative to traditional atomistic or continuum simulations.
The descriptor-based model improves predictive accuracy relative to traditional atomistic or continuum simulations.
The approach will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 20% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related parameters.
The approach will reduce computational time by up to an order of magnitude.
Conventional full atomistic or continuum simulations generally require extensive computational resources.
Conventional simulations have lower predictive accuracy because they do not incorporate hierarchical microstructural descriptors.
High-temperature phase separation or diffusion-driven evolution can alter a high-entropy-alloy microstructure.
Temperature and loading conditions can change deformation mechanisms and microstructural evolution in high-entropy alloys.
Predictive gains may be lost if the descriptors omit critical deformation mechanisms.
Predictive gains are expected only while the hierarchical microstructure remains intact.
The model is to be compared with a conventional full-resolution workflow using measured Young's modulus, yield strength, fracture toughness, computational time, and microstructural stability.
Failure to achieve both at least 20% greater predictive accuracy and roughly a tenfold reduction in computational time is declared a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is restricted to conditions under which the hierarchical microstructure remains intact, but the falsification rule treats significant microstructural evolution as falsification. Evolution outside the stated applicability domain would establish a boundary violation, not decisively refute the in-domain hypothesis.

The outcome promises computational savings of 'up to' one order of magnitude, which allows gains below tenfold, whereas the falsification rule appears to require roughly an order-of-magnitude reduction.
